finding.claim: Unsafe Marshal.load on unauthenticated request parameter in POST /restore enables deserialization of attacker-chosen objects, with RCE dependent on gadget chains in the loaded bundle and DoS regardless. Severity CRITICAL (candidate; gadget chain not verified).
finding.source: params[:state] on POST /restore (app.rb:5), attacker-controlled, base64-decoded at app.rb:6
finding.sink: Marshal.load at app.rb:6; state.inspect reflected at app.rb:7

trace.note: post "/restore" route registered with no auth filter
params[:state] read from request (body or query, attacker-controlled)
Base64.decode64 decodes input; no validation, invalid chars silently ignored
state.inspect returned as response body (text/html by Sinatra default)

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization on route. No format/type validation. No HMAC/signature over blob. No body size limit. Rack::Protection (Sinatra default) does not cover deserialization; its HttpOrigin/RemoteToken checks only block cross-site browser requests, not direct clients. Sinatra default bind 0.0.0.0 means network-reachable.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 declares `post "/restore"` with no before-filter, auth check, or signature/HMAC; app.rb:6 passes `params[:state]` straight through `Base64.decode64` into `Marshal.load` with no validation or size limit. The only file in the directory is app.rb, so no other middleware or auth is defined here. Rack::Protection is a gem default outside this code and does not address deserialization.
verdict.reason: The POST /restore route at app.rb:5 has no authentication and passes attacker-supplied params[:state] into Marshal.load at app.rb:6 with no guard, so any anonymous HTTP client can reach the deserialization sink. Trace lines 5–7 match the code. The RCE severity depends on gadget chains and is not established here, but the unauthenticated unsafe deserialization itself is real. The "Sinatra binds 0.0.0.0 by default" claim is a framework-version assumption I could not verify from the directory and should not be relied on.

finding.claim: Attacker-controlled JSON keys from POST /import are reflected unescaped in a text/html response, giving HTML injection. Severity MEDIUM (browser exploitation narrow).
finding.source: JSON object keys in request body read at app.rb:11 (request.body.read, no size limit)
finding.sink: data.keys.join(",") at app.rb:12 returned with Sinatra default text/html content type

trace.note: request.body.read reads full body unbounded; JSON.parse yields Hash with attacker-chosen string keys
data.keys.join(",") joins keys into response string (sink, no encoding)

finding.guards_checked: No output HTML escaping. No explicit Content-Type override (default text/html). Rack::Protection HttpOrigin blocks most cross-site browser POSTs when Origin header present, so browser-victim exploitation is narrow; same-origin and non-browser clients not blocked. No key allowlist or validation.

verdict.guard_found: Sinatra's default Rack::Protection stack (HttpOrigin) is enabled for this classic-style app. It is not in the repo and I did not read the gem source. It rejects cross-site browser POSTs that carry a mismatched Origin header, which is the only realistic route for injecting into a victim's browser. No output escaping or Content-Type override exists in app.rb.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: app.rb:11 parses the unauthenticated body and app.rb:12 returns the joined keys as text/html with no escaping. The only realistic victim path is a cross-site browser POST, which the default Rack::Protection HttpOrigin check (not in app.rb:10-13; assumed from Sinatra defaults, unverified) blocks, leaving only self-injection into the requester's own response, so the claimed impact does not hold.

finding.claim: Unbounded request body read, uncaught NoMethodError on non-Hash JSON (array or scalar), and development-mode exception exposure. Severity LOW.
finding.source: Request body size and JSON top-level type on POST /import (app.rb:11); nil params[:state] on POST /restore (app.rb:6)
finding.sink: request.body.read memory allocation at app.rb:11; data.keys at app.rb:12 raising NoMethodError; Base64.decode64(nil) at app.rb:6 raising

trace.note: request.body.read with no size limit; JSON.parse on attacker body
data.keys raises NoMethodError when data is Array or scalar, producing 500
Base64.decode64 on nil raises when state param absent; exception shown in development mode

finding.guards_checked: No body size limit. No type check on parsed JSON. RACK_ENV not set in this file, so Sinatra development mode and show_exceptions depend on deployment config (outside audited scope).

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:11 reads request.body with no size limit, and app.rb:12 calls data.keys on the parsed JSON with no type check. app.rb:6 passes params[:state] straight into Base64.decode64 with no nil check or rescue. The file contains no rescue, no error handler, and no authentication. Whether dev-mode exception pages are shown depends on Sinatra config outside app.rb, which I could not verify.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: app.rb:11 reads the unbounded body, and app.rb:12 calls data.keys, which raises NoMethodError on a JSON array or scalar, while app.rb:6 raises on a missing state param, with no guard in the file. The attacker is anonymous, and the impact is a 500 error and possible exception disclosure in development mode (Sinatra's default when RACK_ENV is unset), so the LOW-severity claim holds, though the dev-mode exposure part is unverifiable from this file alone. The candidate omits that app.rb:6 also runs Marshal.load on attacker-controlled input, which is a far more severe issue and should be reported separately.
